legal_question: Is a contract valid if one party lacks legal capacity due to age?
facts: Contract involves purchase of expensive item
legal_analysis: Contract capacity requires parties to be of legal age (18 in most states)
Minors generally lack capacity to enter binding contracts
Contracts with minors are typically voidable at minor's option
Misrepresentation of age does not cure incapacity
legal_conclusion: Contract is likely voidable due to minor's lack of legal capacity, regardless of age misrepresentation

case_precedents.principle: Minor can disaffirm contract even after misrepresenting age

legal_question: What constitutes negligence in a medical malpractice case?
facts: Doctor failed to diagnose obvious symptoms
Patient suffered harm due to delayed treatment
Standard medical protocols were not followed
legal_analysis: Medical negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damages
Duty established by doctor-patient relationship
Breach shown by deviation from standard of care
Causation requires but-for and proximate cause
Damages must be actual and foreseeable
legal_conclusion: Negligence likely established if expert testimony confirms breach of medical standard of care

case_precedents.principle: Standard of care determined by reasonable medical practice

legal_question: Does prior restraint of speech violate the First Amendment?
facts: No immediate clear and present danger
legal_analysis: Prior restraint is presumptively unconstitutional
Government bears heavy burden to justify restraint
National security alone insufficient without imminent harm
Strict scrutiny applies to content-based restrictions
applicable_laws: Supreme Court precedents on prior restraint
legal_conclusion: Prior restraint likely unconstitutional without showing of imminent and irreparable harm to national security

case_precedents.case_name: New York Times Co. v. United States
case_precedents.principle: Heavy presumption against prior restraint of speech

legal_question: Can an employee be terminated for refusing to work overtime?
facts: No union contract or employment agreement
legal_analysis: At-will employment allows termination for any lawful reason
Employer can generally require reasonable overtime
Refusal to work overtime is typically valid grounds for termination
No public policy exception applies to overtime refusal
legal_conclusion: Termination for overtime refusal is likely lawful under at-will employment doctrine

case_precedents.case_name: Payne v. Western & Atlantic Railroad Co.
case_precedents.principle: At-will employees may be discharged for good cause, bad cause, or no cause

legal_question: Is a liquidated damages clause enforceable?
facts: Actual damages difficult to estimate at formation
legal_analysis: Liquidated damages must be reasonable estimate of actual harm
Amount must be difficult to determine at contract formation
Clause will be enforced if not punitive in nature
Courts examine reasonableness at time of contract formation
legal_conclusion: Liquidated damages clause likely enforceable if reasonable approximation of anticipated harm

case_precedents.case_name: Wasserman's Inc. v. Township of Middletown
case_precedents.principle: Liquidated damages enforceable if reasonable and harm difficult to estimate

legal_question: What are the elements of adverse possession?
facts: True owner was aware but took no action
legal_analysis: Adverse possession requires actual, open, notorious, exclusive, and continuous possession
Possession must be hostile (without owner's permission)
Statutory period must be satisfied (varies by state)
Possessor must claim right to property
legal_conclusion: Adverse possession likely established if all elements met for statutory period

case_precedents.principle: Adverse possession requires all statutory elements for continuous period

legal_question: Does corporate veil piercing require fraud?
facts: No fraud or intentional wrongdoing proven
legal_analysis: Veil piercing requires showing corporation is alter ego of shareholders
Factors include undercapitalization, commingling, and lack of formalities
Fraud not always required, but inequitable result must be shown
Courts reluctant to pierce absent compelling circumstances
legal_conclusion: Veil piercing possible based on alter ego theory without requiring proof of fraud

case_precedents.principle: Veil piercing available when corporation is alter ego and inequity results

legal_question: Is specific performance available for breach of contract?
facts: Contract involves sale of unique artwork
Seller refuses to transfer despite payment
legal_analysis: Specific performance is equitable remedy for contract breach
Available when monetary damages inadequate
Requires unique subject matter or special circumstances
Court has discretion to grant or deny relief
legal_conclusion: Specific performance likely available for unique artwork where damages inadequate

case_precedents.principle: Specific performance granted for unique goods where damages inadequate

legal_question: What constitutes reasonable suspicion for Terry stop?
facts: Person in high-crime area late at night
legal_analysis: Terry stop requires reasonable suspicion of criminal activity
Suspicion must be based on specific and articulable facts
Location and time alone insufficient for stop
Nervous behavior in presence of police not necessarily suspicious
legal_conclusion: Reasonable suspicion likely not established based solely on location and nervous behavior

case_precedents.principle: Reasonable suspicion requires specific articulable facts supporting inference of criminal activity

legal_analysis: Non-compete enforceability varies significantly by state
Generally requires reasonable scope in time, geography, and activity
Must protect legitimate business interest
Courts balance employer interests against employee mobility
applicable_laws: Common law restraint of trade principles
legal_conclusion: Enforceability depends on reasonableness of scope and legitimate business interests protected

case_precedents.principle: Non-compete must be reasonable in scope and protect legitimate business interest

legal_question: Does Miranda warning requirement apply to custody?
facts: Told he was free to leave
legal_analysis: Miranda applies to custodial interrogation
Custody determined by whether reasonable person would feel free to leave
Police station setting suggests custody
Statement that person free to leave weighs against custody
legal_conclusion: Custody determination requires analysis of totality of circumstances

case_precedents.principle: Warnings required for custodial interrogation to protect Fifth Amendment rights

legal_question: Is hearsay evidence admissible under excited utterance exception?
facts: Statement made immediately after car accident
Speaker was visibly shaken and emotional
legal_analysis: Excited utterance exception requires startling event
Statement must be made while under stress of excitement
Statement must relate to startling event
Time gap between event and statement relevant
legal_conclusion: Statement likely admissible as excited utterance if made while under stress of accident

case_precedents.principle: Excited utterance requires statement made while under influence of startling event

legal_question: Can trademark rights be acquired through use?
facts: Business used mark in commerce for 5 years
legal_analysis: Trademark rights can be acquired through actual use in commerce
Use must be bona fide commercial use
Rights limited to geographic area of use
Federal registration provides additional benefits
legal_conclusion: Common law trademark rights likely established through continuous commercial use

case_precedents.case_name: United Drug Co. v. Theodore Rectanus Co.
case_precedents.principle: Trademark rights acquired through actual use in commerce

legal_question: What constitutes substantial performance of contract?
facts: Owner refuses to pay citing incomplete performance
legal_analysis: Substantial performance doctrine excuses minor breaches
Performance must achieve essential purpose of contract
Minor deviations do not defeat substantial performance
Non-breaching party entitled to damages for incomplete performance
legal_conclusion: Substantial performance likely achieved, entitling contractor to payment minus damages for deviations

case_precedents.principle: Substantial performance excuses minor breaches that don't defeat contract purpose

legal_question: Is involuntary manslaughter distinct from murder?
facts: No intent to kill or cause serious harm
Defendant aware of risk but proceeded
legal_analysis: Involuntary manslaughter requires reckless or negligent conduct
No intent to kill required unlike murder
Conscious disregard of substantial risk sufficient
Lesser included offense of murder charges
legal_conclusion: Involuntary manslaughter charge appropriate for reckless conduct causing death without intent

case_precedents.principle: Involuntary manslaughter requires proof of criminal negligence or recklessness
